title: The yield imperative: Rethinking success in AI infrastructure
summary: The post The yield imperative: Rethinking success in AI infrastructure appeared first on Source .
body_markdown:
Read in[Traditional Chinese](https://news.microsoft.com/source/asia/2026/09/02/the-new-imperative-for-ai-infrastructure-useful-yield/?lang=zh-hant)


At SEMICON Taiwan 2026, Rani Borkar, President of Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure at Microsoft, called for a new measure of progress as the industry enters the next phase of AI infrastructure. After years defined by the expansion of datacenters, silicon, memory and power, she urged the industry to focus on the “yield imperative”: defining success in AI infrastructure not only on how much capacity it can build, but on how efficiently those resources can be converted into useful intelligence.


At SEMICON Taiwan 2026, Rani Borkar, President of Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure at Microsoft, called for a new measure of progress as the industry enters the next phase of AI infrastructure.


Meeting today’s infrastructure demand requires both more capacity and greater “useful yield”—how efficiently silicon, memory, networking and power translate into useful output, measured through gains such as more tokens per dollar and watt, higher throughput and lower latency.


As each new generation of AI demands more silicon, memory, power and networking, capacity alone will not be enough. Progress involves improving each layer of cloud architecture for efficiency, while discovering disruptive breakthroughs that can only come from crossing domains. This requires collaboration across the global semiconductor ecosystem, from component, equipment and materials providers to utilities, datacenter operators, model builders and software developers.


Microsoft’s experience designing and operating AI infrastructure at global scale points to cross-layer design as the next efficiency frontier. Rather than optimizing components in isolation, companies will need to challenge assumptions and engineer across silicon, memory, networking, power, cooling, software, models, workloads and fleet operations—because the toughest constraints are often solved beyond the layer where they first appear.


Microsoft’s experience designing and operating AI infrastructure at global scale points to cross-layer design as the next efficiency frontier.


*“We will continue to build capacity because the world will need it. But our defining measure of progress must be what comes out: not only chips or tokens, but useful intelligence translated into empowerment, opportunity and human achievement,” said Rani Borkar, President of Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure at Microsoft.*


Microsoft’s goal is not simply to generate more tokens or deploy more infrastructure, but to make intelligence increasingly affordable, dependable and broadly available. When more people and organizations can access intelligence, build on it and create value of their own, infrastructure progress translates into broader economic opportunity and human impact.


Rani Borkar urged the industry to focus on the “yield imperative”: defining success in AI infrastructure not only on how much capacity it can build, but on how efficiently those resources can be converted into useful intelligence.


**Key themes from Microsoft’s SEMICON Taiwan keynote**


- The next phase of AI infrastructure will be defined by useful yield, not raw capacity alone.
- Agentic AI is creating new demands across computing infrastructure.
- Microsoft is taking a silicon-to-systems approach spanning silicon, memory, networking, power and software.
- Continued ecosystem collaboration will be required to improve the efficiency, affordability and reach of AI.


**Microsoft’s approach to the Azure AI infrastructure stack:**


- **Memory: more intelligence from every byte** – Advances in model optimization, memory management, silicon design and compiler placement are integrated to improve the useful intelligence delivered from existing memory resources on the Azure Maia accelerator platform.
- **Networking: designing across layers** – Azure Maia combines two-tier scale-up network topology and a custom transport layer with a network interface card (NIC) integrated directly into the silicon, improving workload flexibility and efficiency to keep compute more productive with less networking hardware.
- **Power: codesigning for efficiency, from grid to chip** – Microsoft is taking an approach to power delivery and management that utilizes hardware-software codesign to maintain performance at less power. For instance, finer-grained power control programmed directly onto the silicon in Microsoft’s Azure Cobalt custom CPU enables significantly more servers to run from the same number of megawatts.
